data.body:
What's new in this guide

Your voice file and your About Me file, filled in for an example person, so you can see what finished ones look like. Ten letter requests written out in full. And the check before you send. Teach ChatGPT how you sound once, and every letter starts closer to your own.

Three of the ten, first lines

A client letter. Something has changed for a client: a delay, a price, a date.

What happened: [the change, in one or two sentences].

Why: [the reason, in a sentence].

What happens next: [the new date, price or step].

See it in fullClose

When you'd send it. Something has changed for a client: a delay, a price, a date. You want them to hear it from you, plainly.

Paste this

Using my voice file and my About Me file, write a short letter to [name], a client who [one line about them and how long we have worked together].

What happened: [the change, in one or two sentences].

Why: [the reason, in a sentence].

What happens next: [the new date, price or step].

What I need from them: [nothing / a reply by a date / a decision].

Under [150] words. Lead with the news, then the reason, then the next step. Don't apologize more than once.

Use only the facts I've given you. If something you need is missing, ask me before you write.

A good answer looks like this. The news comes in the first two sentences. The reason is one sentence. It ends with the next step and your usual sign-off. It doesn't promise anything you didn't.

Check before you send. Is every date and amount the one you gave it? Did it add a reassurance you can't stand behind, such as "there will be no extra cost"?

An email to a supplier. Orders are late or wrong, and you want it fixed without burning the relationship.

The problem: [what went wrong, with numbers, such as "three of the last five orders arrived late"].

The orders: [order or PO numbers, the dates they were due and the dates they arrived].

What it cost us: [one line, such as "we missed a customer's date"].

See it in fullClose

When you'd send it. Orders are late or wrong, and you want it fixed without burning the relationship.

Paste this

Using my voice file and my About Me file, write an email to [name], our contact at [supplier].

The problem: [what went wrong, with numbers, such as "three of the last five orders arrived late"].

The orders: [order or PO numbers, the dates they were due and the dates they arrived].

What it cost us: [one line, such as "we missed a customer's date"].

What I want: [a call this week / a written plan by a date / a credit].

We want to keep working with them. Firm and specific, not angry. Under [150] words.

Use only the facts I've given you. If something you need is missing, ask me before you write.

A good answer looks like this. It states the problem with your numbers, says what it cost, asks for one clear thing by a date, and stays polite.

Check before you send. Are the numbers yours, unchanged? Did it threaten anything you won't do?

A short report to a board or committee. You need to update a board, a committee or a group of members, and they'll skim it.

Here are my notes: [paste your rough notes, figures and dates, or a small table of income and expenses].

Keep every fact and number from my notes exactly as written. Don't add any figure that isn't in my notes. Flag any part of my notes that was unclear with [CHECK].

See it in fullClose

When you'd send it. You need to update a board, a committee or a group of members, and they'll skim it.

Paste this

Using my voice file and my About Me file, write a short report to [the board / committee] of [organization].

Here are my notes: [paste your rough notes, figures and dates, or a small table of income and expenses].

Turn my notes into a report they can read in two minutes. Start with what they need to decide, if anything. Then what happened, then what's next.

Keep every fact and number from my notes exactly as written. Don't add any figure that isn't in my notes. Flag any part of my notes that was unclear with [CHECK].

Under [250] words.

Use only the facts I've given you. If something you need is missing, ask me before you write.

A good answer looks like this. The decision, if there is one, comes first. Every number matches your notes. Anything it wasn't sure of is marked [CHECK] for you to fix.

Check before you send. Put your notes beside the draft and tick off every number. Search the draft for [CHECK].

The ten letters

  • A client letter
  • An email to a supplier
  • A short report to a board or committee
  • A grant paragraph
  • A reference letter
  • A complaint to a company
  • A request to a landlord or service provider
  • A polite no
  • A thank-you to a colleague
  • A follow-up after no reply

Each one ends with the same two lines: "Use only the facts I've given you. If something you need is missing, ask me before you write."

The check before you send

Before your name goes on it, you check that every fact is one you gave it, take out anything it added that you can't stand behind, ask it what it guessed, and read it aloud.

What it is

A PDF guide, written for ChatGPT's free plan, for your own use. Instant download plus an email. A 30-day money-back guarantee covers this purchase: email elvin@elvinpeters.com within 30 days for a full refund. Prices are in US dollars.
